## Programming {.center}

> The implementation of logic to facilitate specified computing operations and functionality

## What we will cover

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   Writing functions, and when not to
-   Conditional Execution
-   Defining Function Arguments
-   Explicit Constraints
-   Dot-dot-dot (...)
-   Pipes
:::

-   Iterations with purrr
-   Anonymous functions and shortcuts

## The cleaning thread {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)

# your own work from last session, if you have it
my_file <- "my_work/cohort_after_s5.rds"

cohort <- if (file.exists(my_file)) {
  read_rds(my_file)
} else {
  # missed the session, or lost the file? start from the provided checkpoint
  read_rds("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/H-Mateus/Data-for-Life-Sciences-in-R/main/data/checkpoints/cohort_after_s5.rds")
}
```

The `if` is there so nobody gets stranded. If you have your own file it is used;
if not, you pick up from a checkpoint and carry on.

## Package load and conflicts

-   We'll load our packages early as is good practise!
-   As an aide, you may notice a verbose message when loading the tidyverse mentioning conflicts
-   If we load the `conflicted` package it will force an error if you use a function that has multiple sources (`filter` is commonly guilty of this!)

```{r}
#| message: true
library(tidyverse)
library(conflicted)
```

## Package load and conflicts

```{r}
#| error: true
# conflicted will make this error
mtcars |>
  filter(gear == 4)
```

```{r}
# We can explicitly state which filter we prefer just once
conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter)

mtcars[1:3,] |>
  filter(gear == 4)
```

## Functions {.smaller}

Functions in R:

- allow you to automate tasks in a more powerful way than copy/paste
- mean you only need to update code in one place
- reduce the likelihood of errors
- are for others, but mainly for **YOU**
- should be written for **readability** and **reusability**
- have the format
```{r}
#| eval: false
function_name <- function(arg1, arg2, arg3) {
  # function body
}
```

## Functions - Practice! {.smaller}
_call your functions after creating them to check their output_

- write an empty function with no arguments, called 'stub_func'.
- write a function that takes no arguments and returns the number 3 using the `return()` statement. Choose an appropriate name.
- create another function with no return statement or arguments, which only contains the number 3. Run the function. Is it different to before?
- create a function called `my_divide()` which takes two arguments, 'x' and 'y' and returns x divided by y. Use an explicit return statement.
- we want to still return a value when y is zero. Change the `my_divide()` function so that there is another argument called 'tol'. Set it to a very low value, and add it to y before dividing.

## General Rules for Writing Functions {.smaller}

Try to decipher the following code below
- what does it do?
- does it work? Are there errors?
```{r}
#| eval: false
df <- data.frame(a = rnorm(10), b = rnorm(10), c = rnorm(10), d = rnorm(10))
df$a <- (df$a - min(df$a, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(df$a, na.rm = TRUE) - min(df$a, na.rm = TRUE))
df$b <- (df$b - min(df$b, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(df$b, na.rm = TRUE) - min(df$a, na.rm = TRUE))
df$c <- (df$c - min(df$c, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(df$c, na.rm = TRUE) - min(df$c, na.rm = TRUE))
df$d <- (df$d - min(df$d, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(df$d, na.rm = TRUE) - min(df$d, na.rm = TRUE))
```

## General Rules for Writing Functions

Is this better?
```{r}
#| eval: false
rescale <- function(x) {
    return((x - min(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - min(x, na.rm = TRUE)))
}
```

## General Rules for Writing Functions

Even better?
```{r}
#| eval: false
rescale <- function(x) {
    y <- min(x, na.rm = TRUE)
    return((x - y) / (max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - y))
}
```

## General Rules for Writing Functions

Perfect?
```{r}
#| eval: false
rescale <- function(x) {
  # rescale vector to the range from 0 to 1
  min_value <- min(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  return((x - min_value) / (max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - min_value))
}
```

## General Rules for Writing Functions
- **_never_** take variables created _outside_ a function and use them from _inside_ a function unless you pass them as an argument
- if you have a lot of functions, it's good practice to put them in a separate file and use 'source'
- generally, functions should do one thing, but you can do whatever you like, including nested functions

## When to write a function
- if you find yourself writing/pasting the same thing 2/3 times

## When NOT to write a function
- if it's a one-off bit of code you'll never use again
- you're lazy
- you hate future you

## Conditional Execution

-   In R, the conditional execution of statements are performed within `if()` and `{}` blocks of code.
-   To start with, code is easier to understand (by you and everyone!) if you separate the lines and use indentations. Not like this:

``` r
myFunction <- function(x) {if (x > 3) {return(x - 3)} else {return(x)}} 
```

-   Note that RStudio has a shortcut for auto-formatting highlighted code: ctrl+shift+A

``` r
myFunction <- function(x) {
  if (x > 3) {
    return(x - 3)
  } else {
    return(x)
  }
}
```

## Conditional Execution | `else if`
We can add multiple `else if` statements to these
```{r}
#| eval: false
if (x > 0) {
    print("Positive")
} else if (x < 0) {
    print("Negative")
} else {
    print("Zero")
}
```

## Conditional Execution | vectorised {.smaller}
- `ifelse()` lets us use vectorised if-else statements, but `dplyr::if_else()` is stricter and keeps types — remember Exhibit F from last session, where `ifelse()` turned dates into numbers
- if you have a lot of `if` statements, `switch()` is next
- `dplyr::case_when()` handles multiple vectorised `if_else()` statements

```{r}
# example use of case_when to simplify multiple if_else statements
mtcars |>
  mutate(mpg_category = case_when(
    mpg < 15 ~ "Low",
    mpg <= 25 ~ "Medium",
    .default = "High"
  )) |>
  select(mpg, mpg_category) |>
  head(3)
```

## Conditional Execution | `switch()`

-   A chain of `else if` branches that all test the *same* variable is a common pattern, and an ugly one:

``` r
if (how == "mean") {
  mean(x)
} else if (how == "median") {
  median(x)
} else if (how == "sd") {
  sd(x)
}
```

-   `switch()` does the same job in a fraction of the space

## `switch()` {.smaller}

-   It takes a value, then one named branch per possible value

```{r}
summarise_by <- function(x, how = c("mean", "median", "sd")) {
  how <- match.arg(how)
  switch(how,
    mean   = mean(x),
    median = median(x),
    sd     = sd(x)
  )
}

v <- c(2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9)

summarise_by(v, "median")
```

-   `match.arg()` is doing the input validation for you: it accepts only the listed options, and defaults to the first

## `switch()` - why bother {.smaller}

-   Ask for something that isn't on the list:

```{r}
#| error: true
summarise_by(v, "mode")
```

-   You get a clear error naming the valid options, and you did not have to write a single check yourself
-   Compare that with an `else if` chain that has no final `else`: it silently returns `NULL`

. . .

**The general principle again:** prefer the construct that fails immediately and
loudly over the one that fails quietly later.

## Defining Function Arguments

-   There are two types of arguments: **Mandatory** and **Optional**
-   The mandatory arguments are **always at the beginning** of the list of arguments, followed by **optional arguments** and their **default values**.
-   Example:

``` r
pow <- function(x, y = 2) {
return(x ** y)
}
```

-   What do you think will happen if you try `pow(3)` and `pow(3,3)` in the console? Try it!

## Defining Function Arguments

-   There are two ways of passing the values to a function: by order and by name.
-   Check the description of `mean()` by typing `?mean`
-   Passing unnamed arguments by order is [**bad programming**]{style="color:#cc0000"} because it means you have to remember the command and each of its arguments (try doing that for 1000 functions!), and it makes your code much less clear!
-   Passing them by name means you can change the order
-   Best practice is to define include the first argument (can be without name) of the function as the input data to be processed:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2|3"
mean(1:101, ,TRUE) # bad!
mean(na.rm = TRUE, x = 1:101) # better
mean(1:101, na.rm = TRUE) # best :)
```

## Defining Function Arguments

-   Adding restrictions to the function means they can be more efficient
-   For example:

```{r}
midValue <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) %% 2 == 0) {
    stop("'x' has an even number of elements", call. = FALSE)
  }
  midIndex <- (length(x) + 1) / 2
  return (x[midIndex])
}
```

-   The stop function is executed when the modulus (remainder from division) is zero. A good error checking mechanism (even gives a message!)

## Defining Function Arguments

-   The previous code can be simplified by using: `stopifnot()`

```{r}
midValue <- function(x) {
  stopifnot("'x' has an even number of elements" = length(x) %% 2 == 1)
  midIndex <- (length(x) + 1) / 2
  return (x[midIndex])
}
```

-   And we can add multiple expressions in one go

```{r}
calMean = function(x) {
  stopifnot(exprs = {
    "'x' has to have a mean of 4 for some reason..." = mean(x) == 4
    "'x' has to have length 4, don't ask why..." = length(x) == 4
  })
  mean(x)
}
```

## Dot-Dot-Dot (...)

-   An ellipsis means that the function can take any number of named or unnamed arguments (run `?print()` for an example)
-   For example: We can use ... to pass those additional arguments on to another function. Essentially, placeholders for other arguments.

```{r}
i01 <- function(y, z) {
  list(y = y, z = z)
}
i02 <- function(a, ...) {
  # Add 'a' to all elements in the list
  lapply(i01(...), function(x) x + a)
}
str(i02(a = 1, y = 2, z = 3))
```

## Dot-Dot-Dot (...)

-   By adding numbers at the end, it is possible to refer to elements of ... by position (what position the generic arguments will sit in).

```{r}
i03 <- function(...) {
  list(first = ..1, third = ..3)
}
str(i03(1, 2, 3))
```

-   More useful is `list(...)`, which evaluates the arguments and stores them in a list. Very useful when working with data!

```{r}
i04 <- function(...) {
  list(...)
}
str(i04(a = 1, b = 2))
```

## Pipes |>

-   There are two types of pipeable functions: **transformations** and **side-effects**.
-   **Transformations** are where an object is passed to the function’s first argument and a modified object is returned.
-   With **side-effects**, the passed object is not transformed. Instead, the function performs a function on that object, such as drawing a plot or saving a file.

```{r}
print_missings <- function(df) {
  n <- sum(is.na(df))
  cat("Missing values: ", n, "\n", sep = "")
  invisible(df)
}
```

## Pipes |>

-   If we use our newly created `print_missings()` function, the `invisible()` command means that the input data frame will not get printed out but we can still use it in a pipe.

```{r}
diamonds |>
  print_missings() |>
  mutate(carat = ifelse(carat < 0.25, NA, carat)) |>
  print_missings()
```

## Iterations with purrr

![](/./10_resources/00_images/purrr_logo.png){.absolute top=-20 right=50 width="80" height="80"}

-   We want to keep code **efficient** and **less repetitive**: performing the same thing on multiple inputs, repeating the operation on multiple columns, or on different datasets.
-   To help achieve this, **iterations** are used. For example:

```{r}
rescale <- function(x) {
  y <- min(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  return((x - y) / (max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - y))
}
```

. . .

```{r}
df <- data.frame(a = rnorm(10), b = rnorm(10), c = rnorm(10), d = rnorm(10))
df$a <- rescale(df$a)
df$b <- rescale(df$b)
df$c <- rescale(df$c)
df$d <- rescale(df$d) # Wow this is tedious...
```

## `for` loops

-   A `for` loop runs the same code once for each element of a sequence

```{r}
for (gene in c("APOE", "TREM2", "APP")) {
  print(paste("Checking", gene))
}
```

-   `gene` takes each value in turn; the code in `{}` is the **body**
-   Loop over **positions** with `seq_along()`, which is safe even when the input is empty (`1:length(x)` is not: it gives `1 0`)

## `for` loops | fixing the repetition

-   So the copy-and-paste above can be replaced with a for loop

```{r}
for (i in seq_along(df)) {
  df[[i]] <- rescale(df[[i]])
} # This is much shorter (and less error prone)!
```

-   Every language has these, so you need to be able to read them, but in R there is usually a better option

## Why purrr instead of `for`? {.smaller}

A loop makes you manage the *how*: set up the output, track the index, fill it in

```{r}
means <- numeric(length(df)) # you must create the output first
for (i in seq_along(df)) {
  means[i] <- mean(df[[i]])
}
```

`map_dbl()` says only the *what*, and guarantees you get numbers back (it errors
otherwise — remember Exhibit E from last session)

```{r}
means <- map_dbl(df, mean)
df <- df |> mutate(across(everything(), rescale)) # and the rescale loop, with across()
```

-   It is **not** about speed: `map()` is a loop underneath. The gain is fewer places to make a mistake
-   The genuinely fast option is a **vectorised** function, one that works on a whole vector at once — which is why `rescale()` takes a column rather than a single value. See [Advanced R](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/perf-improve.html#vectorise)

## Other loops - purr functions

-   **`purrr`** is a package that helps to enhance R's functional programming toolkit
-   **`purrr`** functions help to break common challenges in list manipulation into independent pieces.
-   Base R has family of functions known as **"apply family"**, that eliminates the need for many common for loops, `apply()`, `lapply()`, `tapply()`
-   **`purrr`** has a family of functions called the **"map family"**.
-   Each function takes a vector as input, applies a function to each piece, and then returns a new vector that has the same length as the input.

## The map family

![](/./10_resources/00_images/purrr_logo.png){.absolute top=-20 right=50 width="80" height="80"}

-   Essentially, map() is the tidyverse equivalent of the base R apply family of functions.
-   The basic syntax is `map(.x, .f, ...)` where:
    -   `.x` is a list, vector or dataframe
    -   `.f` is a function
    -   `map()` will then apply `.f` to each element of `.x` in turn.

![](/./10_resources/00_images/purrr_map_cartoon.png){fig-align="center" width="600px"}

## The map family

![](/./10_resources/00_images/purrr_logo.png){.absolute top=-20 right=50 width="80" height="80"}

-   We can use the `map` function to compute the mean and standard deviation of previous dataset.

```{r}
# I'm using round here so we don't get so many decimal places printed
map_dbl(df, mean) |> round(digits = 2)
map_dbl(df, sd) |> round(digits = 2)
# And here's the native R sapply equivalent
sapply(df, mean) |> round(digits = 2)
```

. . .

-   And if you see the help page for `map_dbl()` you'll notice the `...` which allows us to pass function arguments:

```{r}
map_dbl(df, mean, na.rm = TRUE) |> round(digits = 2)
```

## The map family

![](/./10_resources/00_images/purrr_logo.png){.absolute top=-20 right=50 width="80" height="80"}

-   We can even use a string or a position (integer) to extract components from the input data - very useful when working with big datasets!

```{r}
x <- list(
  x = list(a = 1, b = 2, c = 3),
  y = list(a = 4, b = 5, c = 6),
  z = list(a = 7, b = 8, c = 9)
)
x |> map_dbl("a")
x |> map_dbl(2)
```

## map_ functions

![](/./10_resources/00_images/purrr_logo.png){.absolute top=-20 right=50 width="80" height="80"}

-   One property of the `map()` function is that it will always return a list.
-   To change the output data type, we can use multiple versions of `map_*()`:
    -   `map_lgl()` returns a logical.
    -   `map_int()` returns a integer vector.
    -   `map_dbl()` returns a double vector.
    -   `map_chr()` returns a character vector.
    -   `map_df()` returns a data frame.

## Anonymous functions {.smaller}
- sometimes we need to package up some code in a function, but we know we'll never need it again
- this is common where we do something trivial, like a simple calculation
- in these cases we often create a function _on the fly_ in the call to another function
- these are called _anonymous functions_ (because we don't name them) or _lambda functions_ (from lambda calculus)
- they're reasonably common in R, especially when using dplyr

## Anonymous functions {.smaller}
- you've already seen these in calls like `summarise(across(...))`!
- the tilde (`~`) is used to create a lambda function, and the dot (`.x`) is used to refer to the input
- you will also see `.` used to refer to the input - this is the same as `.x`
- you can actually use anything you like, but `.` and `.x` are common conventions

```{r}
# example use of an anonymous function with summarise
mtcars |>
  group_by(cyl) |>
  summarise(across(c(mpg, hp, wt), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))
```

## Anonymous functions {.smaller}

- In this way,

```{r}
#| output: false
#| eval: false
~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
```

is equivalent to

```{r}
#| output: false
#| eval: false
function(.x) {
  mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
}
```

## Shortcuts

-   Fit a linear model to each group in a dataset. This example splits up the mtcars dataset into three pieces and fits the linear model to each piece.

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "1-6|7-10|11-14"
models <- mtcars %>%
  # note this is an example where the native R pipe won't work!
  split(.$cyl) |>
  map(function(df) {
    lm(mpg ~ wt, data = df)
  })
# Using tidyverse annonymous function syntax
models2 <- mtcars %>%
  split(.$cyl) |>
  map( ~ lm(mpg ~ wt, data = .))
# And here is the the native R equivalent
models3 <- mtcars %>%
  split(.$cyl) |>
  map(\(df) lm(mpg ~ wt, data = df))
```

## Shortcuts

-   The `.` used in the second example is a placeholder for the dataset we’ve piped in (`mtcars`) so we can access parts of it (via `$`)
-   Note that the placeholder for the native R pipe (`|>`) is a `_`, but it doesn't have the same functionality as the `magritter` pipe! See [here](https://www.tidyverse.org/blog/2023/04/base-vs-magrittr-pipe/) for more info on differences
-   Example: we want to get the $R^2$ from our models

```{r}
models |>
  map(summary) %>%
  map_dbl( ~ .$r.squared)
models |>
  map(summary) |>
  map_dbl(\(model) model$r.squared)
```

## Multiple Arguments

![](/./10_resources/00_images/purrr_logo.png){.absolute top=-20 right=50 width="80" height="80"}

-   `purrr` gives us the option to include more than one input in parallel with `map2()` and `pmap()`.
-   Imagine we would like to simulate some random normal distributions with different means, and each vary, we could do:

```{r}
# Define input lists
mu <- list(5, 10, -3)
sigma <- list(1, 5, 10)
# Generate distributions
map2(mu, sigma, rnorm, n = 5) |>
  str()
```

## Multiple Arguments

-   The code can be understood by the following figure:

![](/./10_resources/00_images/purrr_map2_cartoon.png){fig-align="center" width="600px"}

## Multiple Arguments

-   There is no map3 or map4, so what if we want more than 2 arguments? `purrr` has the function `pmap()` for an arbitrary number of args.

```{r}
#| output-location: column
n <- list(1, 3, 5)
arguments <- list(n, mu, sigma)

arguments |>
  pmap(rnorm) |>
  str()
```

-   We can go even further by increasing the complexity of the problem using the `exec()` function.

```{r}
funcs <- c("runif", "rnorm", "rpois")
params <- list(list(min = -1, max = 1), list(sd = 5), list(lambda = 10))

map2(funcs, params, \(fn, args) exec(fn, !!!args, n = 5)) |>
  str()
```

## walk

-   `walk()` is an alternative to map that we use we call a function for its side effects, disregarding its return value.

```{r}
x <- list(1, "a", 3)
x |>
  walk(print)
```

-   Really useful when outputting datasets in lists! (such as microarray data)
-   Similar to `map()`, purrr also has `walk2()` and `pwalk()`

## walk2

```{r}
#| eval: false
df0 <- tibble(x = 1:3, y = rnorm(3))
df1 <- tibble(x = 1:3, y = rnorm(3))
df2 <- tibble(x = 1:3, y = rnorm(3))
animalFrames <- tibble(animals = c('sheep', 'cow', 'horse'),
                       frames =
                         list(df0, df1, df2))
# Save a list of dataframes
animalFrames %>%
  walk2(
    .x = .$animals,
    .y = .$frames,
    .f = ~ write_csv(.y, str_c("test_", .x, ".csv"))
  )
```

## pwalk

-   `pmap()` and `pwalk()` allow you to provide any number of arguments in a list.

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "1-10|11-14"
# Let's set-up a dataframe and function to use with pwalk
ds_mt <-
  mtcars |>
  rownames_to_column("model") |>
  mutate(am = factor(am, labels = c("auto", "manual"))) |>
  select(model, mpg, wt, cyl, am) |>
  sample_n(3)
foo <- function(model, am, mpg) {
  print(paste("The", model, "has a", am, "transmission and gets", mpg, "mpgs."))
}
# Now we can use pwalk
ds_mt |>
  select(model, am, mpg) |>
  pwalk(.l = _, .f = foo)
```

## While loops

-   You're unlikely to ever use them in a data analysis context (I never have!), but they evaluate their body code until a condition is met
-   **Example**: see how many times we need to flip a coin to get three heads in a row:

```{r}
#| output-location: column
flip_coin <- function() {
  sample(c("T", "H"), 1)
}
numFlips <- 0
numHeads <- 0
while (numHeads < 3) {
  if (flip_coin() == "H") {
    numHeads <- numHeads + 1
  } else {
    numHeads <- 0
  }
  numFlips <- numFlips + 1
}
cat("Number of flips to get 3 heads in a row: ", numFlips)
```

-   [**Beware**]{style="color:#cc0000"} that while loops can crash if the condition being evaluated never becomes false!

## Using your functions
- modularising code
- unit testing
- packages

## Modularising code
- separating code into functions and files makes it easier to re-use across projects
- it also makes it easier to maintain as we know where to go to change them
- testing functions is also easier than testing code spread out in a script and interweaved with results

## Modularising code - practice!
- create a new R script
- create a function in the script called `my_add()` that takes two arguments, `x` and `y` and returns their sum (do not paste it into the terminal!)
- save the R script
- in the console, source the R script with `source("path/to/script.R")`
- run the function with `my_add(2, 3)`

## Types of testing
- there are many ways to test your code! We have:
  + **unit tests** in your local development environment or CI/CD pipeline
  + **integration tests** to check that your code works with other code
  + **quality assurance tests** to check that your code meets a certain standard (usually done by a separate team)
  + **end-to-end tests** to check that your code works in a real-world (production) environment

## Unit Testing {.smaller}
- for testing the smallest unit of code (functions)
- they are simply functions that test your code to make sure it does what it is supposed to
- this can mean it gives the correct output with expected input, but also that it errors as expected when you give it faulty input
- allows you to change your code and quickly check it still works
- allows you to sleep at night
- done in r using the `testthat` package

## Unit testing - practice! {.smaller}
- create a function called `my_multiply()` that takes two arguments, `x` and `y` and returns their product
- write a test for this function that checks that `my_multiply(2, 3)` returns 6
- use the example of my_add below and modify it:

```{r}
#| output: false
#| eval: false
my_add <- function(x, y) {
  return(x + y)
}

testthat::test_that("my_add() works as expected",
{
  testthat::expect_equal(my_add(2, 3), 5)
})
```

## Putting it all together (optional extra homework)
- create a github account
- install `devtools` and `testthat`
- make a personal package following the outline [here](https://r-pkgs.org/whole-game.html)
- add a function to the package for a common task you do (can be simple)
- write test for your function using `testthat`
- push it to github and (double optional) send me the link!
